author: reek
body: A quotation resolves from the local store and nowhere else. The design's order is local store, then a known peer, then a registry, and the last two do not exist -- but the reason they do not is not that the client is hard. It is that there has never been anything on the other end. Nothing in this tree serves a work to anyone. This is the other end.

author: reek
body: What this chapter does NOT do, and must not be quietly extended to do: it does not decide who may ask. Every work in the store is offered to any caller that names its hash. That is a real policy and it is the right one HERE, because a hash is not a name you can guess -- you cannot ask for a work you have not already been told the digest of, and being told the digest is how a quotation gets written in the first place. Serving by-hash is not serving the store.

author: reek
body: Nothing here signs anything, and nothing needs to. The reply is answerable by its own content: the asker hashes what came back and checks it against the hash it asked for. A peer that lies is caught by the addressing, not by trust. That is the same property that lets the import gate treat the transport as untrusted, and it is why this is a small chapter rather than an architecture.

author: reek
body: The index is built once by the caller and handed in. Rebuilding it per request would re-read the whole log for every quotation.

author: reek
body: An empty payload means "not here", and it is not an error. A peer that does not hold a work is the ordinary case; the asker tries the next one.

author: reek
body: The request. There is nothing to it, which is the point of choosing this verb.

author: reek
body: The only part of this exchange that matters for safety.

author: reek
body: A reply is NOT trusted because of who sent it. It is decoded, and the work it carries is hashed, and that hash must equal the hash that was asked for. Anything else is refused -- a peer that sends a different work, a corrupted work, or a work it made up is caught here by arithmetic rather than by reputation. This is what makes an untrusted transport safe to use: the same argument the import gate makes about the `%%QUOTED-WORKS%%` blob.

author: reek
body: It checks the reply's own hash field too. A reply that names a different hash than the one requested is answering a question nobody asked.

author: reek
body: What accept-reply does NOT do is decide whether the work is TRUSTED. It proves the peer answered the question honestly; whether the author is somebody you admit is the gate's question, and the gate already asks it -- signature, pinned key, trust floor. Content addressing and trust are two checks and this chapter owns exactly one of them. Conflating them is how a transport ends up deciding what to believe.
